extracted.intended_audience: news editors, war correspondents, and military public information officers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and practical requirements—explicit and implicit—governing frontline news dispatches during the Korean War: what correspondents may print, what military authorities may forbid, clearance procedures, and the tension between security and press freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid disclosing information of value to the enemy ('aid and comfort to the enemy')
rubrics_metrics.description: MacArthur headquarters: reporters were denied re-entry because they were 'guilty of disclosing information that would be of value to the enemy and would have a bad morale and psychological effect on our own troops.' The army cited Lambert's dispatches as giving 'aid and comfort to the enemy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not disclose operational details, troop vulnerabilities or material that could be exploited by enemy forces; be especially cautious quoting frontline remarks that could be used for enemy propaganda. Note: the term 'aid and comfort to the enemy' was used by military authorities but described in the article as loosely and variably defined, so exercise extra care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe discretion and cooperate with military guidance/requests
rubrics_metrics.description: Headquarters message referenced 'continued failure to observe discretion or cooperation in a dispatch of their files' as ground for barring correspondents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond to official warnings and cooperate with military public information officers when asked; repeated failure to accept warnings or cooperate may be treated as misconduct (the communiqué mentioned 'previous warning and second chance').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid specific banned references (town names, 'cut off' battalion, commanding general by name)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Korea headquarters spokesman warned correspondents not to mention names of certain towns, forbade describing a battalion as 'cut off' and banned reference to the commanding general by name, even while those names sometimes appeared elsewhere in official communiqués.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not publish the particular place names or phrases specified by military information officers (e.g., certain towns, 'cut off' for units, names of commanding generals) when told they are restricted. Where guidance is inconsistent between venues (field vs HQ communiqués), seek clarification before publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sensationalizing or 'making the army look bad'
rubrics_metrics.description: Col. Echols said Kalischer was banned not for inaccuracies but because his stories were called 'sensational' and 'made the army look bad.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor factual, objective reporting over sensational language or framing that could be construed as unduly critical of military leadership or operations. Editors should evaluate tone as well as factual content to reduce charges of sensationalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure factual accuracy and objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Both Lambert's and Kalischer's dispatches were said not to have violated security nor been factually disputed; the Associated Press and United Press stressed their reporters' accounts were 'frank and factual' and in 'the best ... tradition.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain rigorous fact-checking and objective presentation. Even factual reports may be challenged on other grounds, but accurate, restrained reporting strengthens the defense against censorship or bans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to 'basic security safeguards' and clearance procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: The article notes a 'broad outline of basic security safeguards' had been set forth for guidance and that stories submitted to an information officer (e.g., via radio telephone link to Japan) were read and cleared in sequence, sometimes entailing long waits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow whatever basic safeguards and clearance workflows are in place (submit copy to information officers when required, expect delays and queued review). Keep records of submissions and clearances to document compliance if questioned later.

rubrics_metrics.name: When definitions are vague, seek clearer guidance and regular briefings
rubrics_metrics.description: Correspondents repeatedly asked for regular briefings on the military situation and clearer, more complete guidance because 'the definition of security was so loose' among army officers that correspondents could not judge for themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt military headquarters for explicit, consistent definitions of prohibited material and request regular briefings; insist on written or on-the-record clarifications where possible to reduce arbitrary enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer uniform/open censorship to inconsistent, ad hoc restrictions (correspondents' governance preference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many correspondents indicated they 'would prefer open censorship to [the loose]' system; several organizations urged uniform military censorship as had been applied in World War II, arguing it would be a better approach than banning individual reporters under fuzzy rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider advocating for an explicit, uniformly applied censorship regime (if necessary) rather than enduring variable, unpredictable restrictions that risk arbitrary punishment of individual reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish reporting considerations into two categories: military security vs military prestige
rubrics_metrics.description: The piece states the problem falls into two broad categories: (1) military security (leaks about troop movement, locations, etc.), and (2) military prestige (reporting that may harm morale or public perception and thus be seen as aiding the enemy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating whether to publish, separate operational-security risks (which can directly endanger troops) from reports that may damage prestige or morale (which may be grounds for military objection but are more subjective). Apply stricter withholding/personal clearance for clear security risks; treat prestige-related restrictions with clearer standards and editorial deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign military officers conversant with security to work with correspondents / adopt a correspondents' code
rubrics_metrics.description: Lambert said he 'suggested several times to army authorities... that an officer or officers conversant with security and anything which might help the enemy be assigned to work with correspondents' and that 'I helped to frame in Korea a correspondents code.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News organizations and military headquarters should jointly designate liaison officers with security expertise to advise correspondents, and where practicable formalize a correspondents' code to clarify boundaries and expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withhold news developments when publication could cost American soldiers' lives
rubrics_metrics.description: The article reports 'Some newsmen have withheld news developments on the grounds [that] nothing is published which might cost American soldiers,' indicating conscious withholding to protect troops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When in doubt about operational impact, err on the side of withholding specifics that could endanger personnel or missions; document editorial judgments and, if feasible, consult military liaisons for an assessment of likely harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of perception (avoid being labeled 'provocateur' or 'fomenter of war')
rubrics_metrics.description: Lambert noted it was difficult to reconcile army accusations of 'giving aid and comfort' with communist accusations calling him an 'American fomenter of war' and 'provocateur.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond factual accuracy, consider how reporting might be used by different audiences to ascribe motive or effect; avoid rhetoric that could be misinterpreted as advocacy or agitation rather than reporting.
